claim: ILO's 2024 Global Employment Trends for Youth estimates 67 million unemployed youth globally, with youth-to-adult unemployment ratios of 3-4x in many LMICs and skills mismatch identified as a primary barrier to youth employment.
method: Reviewed ILO youth employment report for global and regional youth unemployment estimates, skills-mismatch analysis, and training-coverage data.
limitations: Youth unemployment figures depend on national labor-force survey definitions that vary across countries — what counts as 'unemployed' differs.
The 67 million figure excludes discouraged workers and underemployed youth — the actual youth employment challenge is larger than the headline number suggests.
Skills-mismatch is identified as a barrier but the assessment is based on employer surveys and labor-force data, not direct measurement of skill gaps at individual level.
Sub-national unemployment data is not systematically reported — national averages mask enormous regional variation.

claim: TVET provision in most low- and middle-income countries is diverse and fragmented across government ministries, private providers, and NGOs, which complicates building system-wide data on training providers and their outcomes.

source.title: Building Better Formal TVET Systems: Principles and Practice in Low- and Middle-Income Countries (World Bank, ILO, UNESCO, 2023)

method: Reviewed training-data assessments, provider-registry documentation, and employment-outcome tracking rates across LMICs.
limitations: The originally cited 'Skills training data systems assessment' could not be confirmed to exist; re-sourced to the World Bank/ILO/UNESCO TVET systems report.
This report describes TVET system fragmentation broadly; it does not quantify provider-registry coverage country by country.
A dedicated source is still needed to substantiate the 'no single dataset' claim for any specific country.

claim: ILO's School-to-Work Transition Survey microdata collection covers more than 30 countries surveyed between 2012 and 2016, with individual youth variables and derived employment, unemployment, and school-enrolment measures; an employer labour-demand survey was conducted in seven countries.

source.title: School-to-work transition survey (SWTS) micro data files

method: Reviewed the ILO dataset landing page for survey years, country coverage, youth age range, derived variables, employer-survey linkage, geographic coverage fields, and access instructions.
limitations: The collection is historical, with fieldwork from 2012 to 2016, and cannot represent current labour-market conditions without a newer survey.
Microdata access requires a request to ILOSTAT, so a reviewer cannot assume immediate public download or unrestricted replication.
SWTS measures youth labour-market transitions and training participation but is not a complete training-provider registry.
Country samples and geographic coverage differ; cross-country or sub-national comparisons require survey-specific weights and documentation.
The exact page publication date is used as source_date because the page does not expose a separate dataset release date.

claim: ILO's YouthSTATS database defines youth as ages 15 to 29 and publishes indicators covering labour force participation, employment, unemployment, school-to-work transitions, working time, and earnings, using labour-force and household survey sources.
method: Reviewed the YouthSTATS scope, youth-age definition, listed indicators, data-source description, school-to-work survey history, and stated policy use before classifying it as a labour-market outcome layer.
limitations: The page does not expose a precise last-updated date; 2022-01-01 is a year-level source-date proxy and must be replaced if metadata becomes available.
YouthSTATS does not enumerate training providers, programme capacity, course content, or provider-level outcome-tracking rates.
Indicators are country or survey based and may not support sub-national analysis in every country.
Definitions and comparability depend on the source survey, national implementation, and the applicable statistical standards.

claim: ILOSTAT derives harmonized informal-employment indicators by processing national household-survey microdata using production-unit and job-formality classifications, generally for the main job; this provides an informal-sector outcome context but does not identify whether a training graduate received or benefited from a specific programme.

source.title: Labour Force Statistics (LFS and RURBAN databases)

method: Reviewed the ILOSTAT informality concepts, 21st International Conference of Labour Statisticians reference, processing path, main-job limitation, and stated policy uses for training and skills development.
limitations: The page does not expose a precise publication or update date; 2023-01-01 is a year-level proxy tied to the cited 2023 statistical resolution.
Informal-employment statistics are not a training-graduate tracer system and cannot attribute outcomes to a provider or programme.
The main-job focus can miss informal second jobs, seasonal work, and mixed livelihoods.
National survey questions, coverage, weights, and adoption of the latest standards vary across countries.
Country-level or modeled estimates must not be presented as sub-national outcome data without the underlying microdata and metadata.

claim: The World Bank STEP Skills Measurement Program combines household and employer surveys to measure cognitive, socio-emotional, job-relevant, training, compensation, and employer-demand indicators, with available data collected from 2012 to 2017 in a defined set of economies and an urban adult target population.
method: Reviewed the STEP collection description for survey components, measured constructs, employer modules, collection dates, country list, target population, and accompanying methodology documentation.
limitations: The listed data were collected between 2012 and August 2017 and may not represent current skills demand or training provision.
The target population is urban adults aged 15 to 64, so rural youth, younger adolescents, and many informal workers are outside the core frame.
STEP does not provide a complete sub-national training-provider registry or programme-level graduate tracer.
Employer and household surveys are separate instruments; linking skills supply, provider participation, and employment outcomes requires additional identifiers or design assumptions.
The source page does not expose a single dataset release date; source_date records the end of the listed collection window.

claim: UNESCO-UNEVOC TVET country profiles provide concise system-level information and comparative statistical context for TVET systems worldwide, making them a useful national policy and provider-system context layer rather than a complete sub-national provider census.

source.title: UNESCO-UNEVOC TVET country profiles - SDG 4 Knowledge Hub

method: Reviewed the UNESCO SDG 4 Knowledge Hub description of the country profiles, dynamic system diagrams, comparative statistical function, data-monitoring classification, and global scope.
limitations: The page does not expose a precise update date; 2026-01-01 is a year-level proxy for the current dynamic resource.
Country profiles describe TVET systems and indicators but do not enumerate every government, NGO, private, or informal training provider.
System-level statistical context does not provide provider-level enrollment, completion, graduate employment, or outcome-tracking rates.
Comparability depends on the national and international sources integrated into each profile and their update cycles.

claim: The World Bank Enterprise Surveys provide nationally representative firm-level data across more than 150 economies, with public aggregated indicators and registered-user microdata covering business performance and employer-side constraints relevant to skills-demand analysis; the catalog records national granularity and 2006-2023 temporal coverage.

source.title: Enterprise Surveys - World Bank Data Catalog

method: Reviewed the World Bank catalog metadata for survey population, economy coverage, national granularity, temporal coverage, public license, indicator files, and microdata access conditions; cross-checked the Enterprise Surveys methodology for formal-firm sampling boundaries.
limitations: The catalog records national granularity, so the dataset cannot automatically locate sub-national training demand or provider gaps.
Formal-sector surveys target registered private firms and therefore omit many informal businesses and own-account activities; separate informal surveys are not interchangeable.
Firm-reported skills constraints measure employer perception and demand, not verified youth skill proficiency or programme effectiveness.
The dataset does not link firms to training providers or individual graduates.
Survey years and question modules vary by economy, so cross-country comparisons require survey-version and indicator audits.

claim: World Bank metadata for Benin's 2017 Youth Employment Project describes a public multi-arm randomized evaluation comparing a comprehensive package, a cash-only arm, and a training-only arm using vulnerable employment, earnings, business profits, and job creation outcomes, with heterogeneity by gender and cognitive and non-cognitive skills.

source.title: Benin - Projet Emploi Jeune Impact Evaluation 2017, Baseline Survey

method: Reviewed the World Bank metadata for study design, treatment arms, outcome fields, heterogeneity dimensions, geographic and temporal coverage, public classification, and research-data license. Treated the record as evaluation-design evidence, not as a result estimate.
limitations: The metadata describes a Benin project and does not establish effects for other countries or training systems.
The catalog entry is labeled a baseline survey and reports no resources available; outcome-file access and follow-up completeness require separate verification.
The trial compares bundled interventions, so a training-only result cannot automatically identify the effect of provider quality or curriculum.
The listed outcomes do not by themselves establish durable employment, informal-sector success, or cost-effectiveness.
